question.text: Chapter 2, Section 2.6 traces the antecedents and growth of alternative investments globally. Which of the following correctly matches the historical milestone described in the chapter?

answer.text: Modern portfolio theory advances of the 1950s-60s established that risk from alternative investments can be diversified in a portfolio context, revolutionising the basket of assets available for institutional investors
Venture capital became fully institutionalised in the UK in the 1600s with the East India Company
The 2008 Global Financial Crisis triggered the permanent DECLINE of alternative investments globally
The dotcom bust of 2001 led to the permanent shutdown of all US venture-capital firms

explanation.text: The Logic: Section 2.6 states: 'Beginning with the 1950s and 1960s, modern portfolio theory made considerable advances which established the mechanics and advantages of diversification advocating the principle that risk from alternative investments can be diversified.' This insight revolutionised the basket of assets — small-caps, unlisted stocks, high-yield debt, structured products became institutionally acceptable on a portfolio basis. The Trap: Option B fabricates VC history — VC institutionalised via US-style professional funds in the 1940s-50s. Option C inverts reality — alternatives EXPANDED post-2008 as traditional returns compressed. Option D similarly over-states — the dotcom bust was a setback but VC recovered and hit a new high-growth curve after 2004 per Section 2.6. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C (All-Cat Manager) and XIX-D (Cat I/II Manager) carry the same history lesson. XV (Research Analyst) tests Markowitz diversification at a more quantitative level. Manager's Pro-Tip: When pitching a new Cat III strategy, anchor it historically: MPT-era diversification insights PLUS post-2008 alpha-scarcity are the two foundational narratives that justify the institutional allocation. If your pitch cannot articulate WHY the strategy earns a premium in a post-MPT, post-QE world, LPs will assume it is a factor tilt in disguise.
